lesson.title: Data ethics: fair, safe and honest
lesson.subtitle: What to collect, who sees it, and how to report it truthfully

video.title: Data ethics: fair, safe and honest
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Amina Bello — primary teacher (opens the lesson)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Amina looks at a dashboard of classroom CO₂ lines; one room's line drops flat every afternoon. The head teacher leans in, pointing.
scenes.animation: The flat stretches highlight one by one.
scenes.narration: Our CO₂ sensors showed something unexpected: which rooms were empty, and when. One room was empty most afternoons, and the head teacher asked whose it was. The data was about air, but it told us about people.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: data ethics, using a project's data fairly, safely and honestly.

scenes.visual: Three sensor icons (air, noise, a door) each draw a line; a timetable slides over the lines and one name lights up.
scenes.animation: The timetable overlays the lines; one cell glows.
scenes.narration: Sensor data is rarely only about things. CO₂ and noise show when a room is full or empty. A door sensor shows when someone comes in early. Put next to a timetable, it can point to one person.

scenes.visual: A form with many boxes; most are crossed out until only 'room', 'CO₂' and 'time' remain.
scenes.animation: Boxes cross out one by one.
scenes.narration: So ask what the project really needs. For fresh air: CO₂ per room, and the time. Not names, not a camera, not who sat where. Every extra piece of data is more to protect and explain.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma raises an eyebrow at a colleague holding a small camera beside a classroom window. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A colleague wants a camera in each classroom, to check the windows get opened. Is it needed?

scenes.visual: A CO₂ line drops sharply at the moment a window icon opens. The camera gets a cross.
scenes.animation: The line falls; the camera fades out.
scenes.narration: No camera needed: when windows open, the CO₂ falls. A camera would film children's faces, which needs far more care and permission. Choose the least data that answers your question.

scenes.visual: A one-page notice for families, in two languages, going home in pupils' bags; a parent signs a slip.
scenes.animation: The notice folds into a bag; a tick appears on the slip.
scenes.narration: Before you start, tell people what you'll collect, why, and who will see it. For anything about people, ask for consent, and for children, ask their parents too. Use plain words, in the language families speak at home.

scenes.visual: Two doors: an open one with a chart of room averages, a locked one with raw readings. A calendar page tears off at the end of term.
scenes.animation: The locked door's key goes to the project team; the calendar page falls.
scenes.on_screen_text: Who sees it, and how long?
scenes.narration: Decide who sees what: everyone sees room averages, only the team sees raw readings. Keep raw data for a term, then delete it. Data protection laws in Kenya, Nigeria and Egypt expect limited access, and no keeping data longer than you need it.

scenes.visual: A results poster for the staffroom with a small 'how sure are we?' box in the corner listing the limits.
scenes.animation: The box's lines tick in one by one.
scenes.narration: Then share what you found, honestly. Say how sure you are: one sensor per room, two weeks of data, a gap during exams. Show the bad news too, and what you removed and why.

scenes.visual: Two speech bubbles over a bar chart: a loud one with a big claim, a calm one with the numbers and the dates.
scenes.animation: The loud bubble shrinks; the calm one settles over the chart.
scenes.narration: Room six has the worst air in the school: that claims too much. Room six went above fifteen hundred ppm on most afternoons we measured: that's honest, and still useful.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holding a printout of room lines, the head teacher's door behind him. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: Hand it to the head teacher?
scenes.narration: Your turn. The head teacher wants the CO₂ data to see which teachers leave their rooms early. The data could show it. Should the project hand it over?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a filter, a signed slip, a padlock, a balance.
scenes.narration: No: people agreed to a project about fresh air, not about watching staff. A new use needs new consent. Remember: only the data you need, ask and explain, limit who sees it and for how long, and report honestly.

scenes.visual: Pupils at desks with a four-column table on the board: need it?, could reveal, who sees, delete when. A short letter to families on the desk.
scenes.animation: The table fills row by row; the letter folds.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: a data audit. For each piece of data, pupils ask: do we need it, what could it reveal, who sees it, and when is it deleted? Then they write a short notice for families. Now lead a project your school can trust.

checkpoints.prompt: To check that windows get opened, a colleague wants a camera in each classroom. Is it needed?

options.text: No — the CO₂ already shows it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — when the windows open, the CO₂ falls, so the sensor already answers the question. A camera would also film children.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the CO₂ reading already falls when the windows open. A camera adds children's faces, which need far more care and consent.

checkpoints.prompt: The head teacher wants the CO₂ data to see which teachers leave their rooms early. Should the project hand it over?

options.text: No — that's not what people agreed to

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — people agreed to a project about fresh air, not to being watched. A new use needs a new conversation and new consent.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the data was collected for fresh air. Using it to watch staff breaks that promise, and people will stop trusting the project.
